lessons.title: Concentration of solutions and titrations
lessons.summary: Master concentration in g/dm³ and mol/dm³, convert between the two, and use titration results to find the unknown concentration of an acid or alkali.
objectives: I can calculate the concentration of a solution in g/dm³ and in mol/dm³.
I can convert between g/dm³ and mol/dm³ using relative formula mass.
I can describe how to carry out a titration accurately.
I can use titration results and a balanced equation to calculate an unknown concentration.

activities.title: Concentration in g/dm³ and mol/dm³
activities.content:
## Two ways to say how strong a solution is

**Concentration** tells you how much solute is dissolved in a certain volume of solution. Chemists use a volume of **1 dm³**, which is the same as **1000 cm³** (one litre).

**In grams per dm³:**

$$\text{concentration (g/dm}^3) = \frac{\text{mass (g)}}{\text{volume (dm}^3)}$$

**In moles per dm³:**

$$\text{concentration (mol/dm}^3) = \frac{\text{moles (mol)}}{\text{volume (dm}^3)}$$

The mol/dm³ version is more useful for reactions, because equations are written in moles.

**Converting the volume:** most lab volumes are in cm³. Divide by 1000 to get dm³. So 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, and 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³.

**Converting between the two concentrations:** they are linked by the Mr, just like mass and moles.

- g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr
- mol/dm³ = g/dm³ ÷ Mr

A solution of sodium hydroxide (Mr = 40) at 2 mol/dm³ is the same as 80 g/dm³.

activities.title: Worked example: finding concentration
activities.content:
**7.3 g of hydrogen chloride is dissolved in water to make 500 cm³ of solution. Find the concentration in g/dm³ and in mol/dm³.** (Mr of HCl = 36.5)

*Step 1: convert the volume.* 500 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.5 dm³

*Step 2: concentration in g/dm³.* 7.3 ÷ 0.5 = **14.6 g/dm³**

*Step 3: convert to moles.* moles of HCl = 7.3 ÷ 36.5 = 0.2 mol

*Step 4: concentration in mol/dm³.* 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = **0.4 mol/dm³**

*Check:* 0.4 mol/dm³ × 36.5 = 14.6 g/dm³ ✓

**The reverse question:** how many moles are in 25 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide?

moles = concentration × volume = 0.1 × 0.025 = **0.0025 mol**

This rearrangement is the one you will use most in titration calculations.

question.text: 20 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
question.hint: First change 250 cm³ into dm³ by dividing by 1000.

question.text: A solution of sulfuric acid has a concentration of 4.9 g/dm³. Calculate its concentration in mol/dm³. (Mr of H₂SO₄ = 98)

activities.title: Carrying out a titration
activities.content:
## The titration method

A **titration** finds exactly what volume of one solution reacts with a measured volume of another. It is used to find an unknown concentration of an acid or alkali.

**Method for titrating an acid against an alkali:**

1. Use a **pipette** to measure 25.0 cm³ of the alkali into a conical flask. A pipette is very accurate for one fixed volume.
2. Add a few drops of a suitable **indicator**, e.g. phenolphthalein (pink in alkali, colourless in acid) or methyl orange (yellow in alkali, red in acid). Universal indicator is not used because its colour changes gradually.
3. Fill a **burette** with the acid and record the starting volume, reading from the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
4. Add acid from the burette while **swirling** the flask. As the end-point approaches, add drop by drop.
5. Stop at the exact colour change (the **end-point**) and record the final volume. The difference is the **titre**.
6. Repeat until you have **concordant** results: titres within 0.10 cm³ of each other. Use the mean of the concordant titres, ignoring the first rough run.

A white tile under the flask makes the colour change easier to see.

question.text: Put the steps of a titration in the correct order.
question.explanation: Pipette the alkali, add indicator, fill the burette and read it, add acid to the end-point, then record and repeat for concordant results.
order: Pipette 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask
Add a few drops of indicator
Fill the burette with acid and record the initial reading
Add acid while swirling until the indicator just changes colour
Record the final reading and repeat until concordant

activities.title: Titration calculations
activities.content:
## From titre to concentration

Once you know the titre, the calculation follows a fixed pattern. Suppose 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.

$NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O$

**Step 1: moles of the known solution.**
moles of HCl = concentration × volume (in dm³) = 0.1 × 0.020 = 0.002 mol

**Step 2: use the equation ratio to find moles of the unknown.**
The ratio is 1:1, so moles of NaOH = 0.002 mol

**Step 3: concentration of the unknown.**
concentration of NaOH = moles ÷ volume = 0.002 ÷ 0.025 = **0.08 mol/dm³**

**Step 4 (if asked): convert to g/dm³.**
0.08 × 40 = 3.2 g/dm³

Watch the ratio in step 2. For $H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O$, each mole of sulfuric acid reacts with **two** moles of sodium hydroxide, so moles of NaOH = 2 × moles of H₂SO₄.

Write out all three steps in the exam. Even if the final number is wrong, the method marks are yours.

activities.title: Worked example: a 1:2 ratio
activities.content:
**25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution needed 15.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid to neutralise it. Find the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³.**

$H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O$

*Step 1:* moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.2 × 0.015 = 0.003 mol

*Step 2:* ratio is 1 H₂SO₄ : 2 NaOH, so moles of NaOH = 2 × 0.003 = 0.006 mol

*Step 3:* concentration of NaOH = 0.006 ÷ 0.025 = **0.24 mol/dm³**

**And in g/dm³?** Mr of NaOH = 40, so 0.24 × 40 = **9.6 g/dm³**

A common slip is dividing by 2 instead of multiplying. Ask yourself: which substance has the bigger number in the equation? That is the one with more moles.

question.text: 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 22.0 cm³ of 0.15 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. $KOH + HCl \rightarrow KCl + H_2O$. Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
question.hint: Moles of HCl = 0.15 × 0.022. Ratio 1:1. Divide by 0.025.
question.explanation: Moles of HCl = 0.15 × 0.022 = 0.0033 mol. Moles of KOH = 0.0033 mol. Concentration = 0.0033 ÷ 0.025 = 0.132 mol/dm³.

activities.title: Accuracy, precision and choosing equipment
activities.content:
## Why the equipment matters

Each piece of titration equipment is chosen for a reason.

| Equipment | Why it is used |
|---|---|
| Volumetric pipette | measures one fixed volume (e.g. 25.0 cm³) very accurately |
| Burette | measures a variable volume to the nearest 0.05 cm³ |
| Conical flask | narrow neck stops splashes when swirling |
| White tile | makes the colour change easier to see |

A measuring cylinder is **not** accurate enough: its markings are typically 1 cm³ apart, which would give a large uncertainty in a 25 cm³ measurement.

**Concordant results** matter because a single titration may overshoot the end-point. Taking the mean of results within 0.10 cm³ of each other reduces the effect of random error. The first "rough" titration is done quickly to find roughly where the end-point is and is not included in the mean.

Common sources of error: not reading the meniscus at eye level, air bubbles in the burette tip, adding acid too fast near the end-point.

question.text: A student's titres are 23.40 cm³, 22.85 cm³, 22.90 cm³ and 22.80 cm³. Which value should be left out when calculating the mean?
question.hint: Concordant results are within 0.10 cm³ of each other.
question.explanation: 23.40 cm³ is much higher than the others (probably the rough run or an overshoot). The other three are concordant, giving a mean of 22.85 cm³.

question.text:
A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution with 0.10 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 18.50 cm³.

$H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O$

(a) Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid in the mean titre. (1 mark)

(b) Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide that reacted. (1 mark)

(c) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³. (1 mark)

(d) Convert your answer to g/dm³. (Mr of NaOH = 40) (1 mark)

(e) Explain why the student used a pipette rather than a measuring cylinder for the sodium hydroxide. (1 mark)
question.hint: 18.50 cm³ = 0.0185 dm³. The ratio is 1 acid : 2 alkali.
question.explanation: (a) 0.10 × 0.0185 = 0.00185 mol. (b) 2 × 0.00185 = 0.0037 mol. (c) 0.0037 ÷ 0.025 = 0.148 mol/dm³. (d) 0.148 × 40 = 5.92 g/dm³. (e) A pipette measures a fixed volume much more accurately than a measuring cylinder, reducing the uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Pipette is more accurate / precise, smaller uncertainty

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Concentration** = mass ÷ volume (g/dm³) or moles ÷ volume (mol/dm³); volume in **dm³** (cm³ ÷ 1000).
- g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr.
- Titration: **pipette** the alkali, add **indicator**, add acid from a **burette** to the end-point, repeat for **concordant** titres (within 0.10 cm³).
- Calculation: moles of known → use equation **ratio** → moles of unknown → divide by its volume.
- Pipettes and burettes are used because they are far more accurate than measuring cylinders.

practiceQuestions.text: What mass of solute is dissolved in 2 dm³ of a 15 g/dm³ solution?
Calculate the number of moles of hydrochloric acid in 50 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ solution.
Why is universal indicator not suitable for a titration?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how sharply its colour changes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Universal indicator changes colour gradually through many shades, so there is no sharp end-point. Phenolphthalein or methyl orange give a single clear colour change.

options.text: Its colour changes gradually, so the end-point is not sharp
It only works with strong acids
It reacts with the glass of the burette

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about titration equipment.

metadata.blanksText: A ___ is used to measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali into the flask. A ___ is used to add the acid a little at a time and measure the volume used.

practiceQuestions.hint: One measures a fixed volume; the other has a tap.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A pipette measures the fixed volume; a burette delivers a variable, measured volume.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: doubling the volume of water a fixed mass of salt is dissolved in halves the concentration.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. The same mass in twice the volume gives half the concentration.

practiceQuestions.text: A solution of sodium carbonate has a concentration of 0.25 mol/dm³. Calculate its concentration in g/dm³. (Mr of Na₂CO₃ = 106)
Explain why a titration is repeated until concordant results are obtained.
practiceQuestions.hint: What could go wrong in a single run, and what does averaging do?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A single titration might overshoot the end-point or contain a random error. Repeating until results agree within 0.10 cm³ shows the result is reliable, and using the mean reduces the effect of random errors.

markScheme.criterion: A single result may contain a random error / overshoot the end-point
Concordant results (within 0.10 cm3) show reliability / mean reduces error

practiceQuestions.text:
25.0 cm³ of a solution of nitric acid was neutralised by 30.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide.

$HNO_3 + NaOH \rightarrow NaNO_3 + H_2O$

(a) Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide used. (1 mark)

(b) Calculate the concentration of the nitric acid in mol/dm³. (2 marks)

(c) Calculate the concentration of the nitric acid in g/dm³. (Mr of HNO₃ = 63) (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: 0.20 × 0.030 for (a). Ratio is 1:1. Then divide by 0.025.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) 0.20 × 0.030 = 0.006 mol. (b) Moles of HNO₃ = 0.006 mol; concentration = 0.006 ÷ 0.025 = 0.24 mol/dm³. (c) 0.24 × 63 = 15.12 g/dm³.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following would make a titration result LESS accurate? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two of these introduce error; two are good practice.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reading the burette from above (not at eye level) and adding acid quickly near the end-point both cause error. Swirling the flask and using a white tile improve the result.

options.text: Reading the burette from above rather than at eye level
Adding the acid quickly near the end-point
Swirling the flask during the titration
options.feedback: Swirling mixes the solutions and is good practice.

options.text: Placing a white tile under the flask
options.feedback: The white tile helps you see the colour change.

practiceQuestions.text: 12 g of potassium nitrate is dissolved in water to make 400 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm³.
practiceQuestions.hint: Convert 400 cm³ to dm³ before dividing.

practiceQuestions.text: A bottle of nitric acid is labelled 12.6 g/dm³. Calculate its concentration in mol/dm³. (Mr of HNO₃ = 63)
practiceQuestions.hint: Divide the concentration in g/dm³ by the Mr to change grams into moles.

practiceQuestions.text: A student is finding the concentration of an acid by titrating it against a known alkali. Put the practical steps in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: The alkali goes in the flask first; you cannot read a titre until the burette has been filled and read.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rinse and fill the burette with acid, transfer the alkali by pipette, add indicator, take the initial reading, run in the acid until the colour just changes, then take the final reading and repeat for concordant titres.
order: Rinse the burette with the acid, fill it and remove any air bubble from the tip
Transfer 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask using a volumetric pipette
Add three drops of methyl orange to the flask
Read the initial burette volume at eye level
Run acid into the flask, swirling, going drop by drop as the colour starts to change
Read the final burette volume and repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³

practiceQuestions.text: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 19.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ nitric acid. $HNO_3 + NaOH \rightarrow NaNO_3 + H_2O$. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
practiceQuestions.hint: Moles of HNO₃ = 0.20 × 0.019. The ratio is 1:1. Divide by the alkali volume in dm³.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Moles of HNO₃ = 0.20 × 0.019 = 0.0038 mol. Ratio 1:1, so moles of NaOH = 0.0038 mol. Concentration = 0.0038 ÷ 0.025 = 0.152 mol/dm³.

practiceQuestions.text: A student records titres of 24.10 cm³, 24.15 cm³, 24.75 cm³ and 24.20 cm³. Which titre should NOT be included in the mean?
practiceQuestions.hint: Only results within 0.10 cm³ of each other are concordant.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 24.75 cm³ is more than 0.5 cm³ above the others, so it is not concordant (probably an overshoot). The other three agree within 0.10 cm³ and give a mean of 24.15 cm³.

practiceQuestions.text:
A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide solution with 0.050 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 21.00 cm³.

$H_2SO_4 + 2KOH \rightarrow K_2SO_4 + 2H_2O$

(a) Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid in the mean titre. (1 mark)

(b) Calculate the number of moles of potassium hydroxide that reacted. (1 mark)

(c) Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide in mol/dm³. (1 mark)

(d) Convert your answer to g/dm³. (Mr of KOH = 56) (1 mark)

(e) Explain why the student added the acid drop by drop as the end-point approached. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: 21.00 cm³ = 0.021 dm³. One mole of acid reacts with two moles of alkali.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) 0.050 × 0.021 = 0.00105 mol. (b) 2 × 0.00105 = 0.0021 mol. (c) 0.0021 ÷ 0.025 = 0.084 mol/dm³. (d) 0.084 × 56 = 4.70 g/dm³. (e) Adding drop by drop stops the student overshooting the end-point, so the titre is accurate.

markScheme.criterion: To avoid overshooting the end-point / to find the exact end-point
